title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: Paired Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and a deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on intent→configuration translation tasks. The preregistered paired design used N = 300 intent→configuration tasks (four intent clusters, 75 tasks each), a shared initial candidate per task supplied to both conditions, and a constrained repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini; deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implementing the full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule. The run completed as preregistered (planned_episode_count = 600; completed_episode_count = 600; model_calls_used = 301). Primary outcomes were baseline 299/300 passes (0.9966667) and guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); the paired contingency was n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0, yielding an observed paired difference = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333, paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered target effect (absolute increase 0.10; ≈80% power at N = 300) was not supported: an arithmetic ceiling produced by a near‑perfect baseline together with the shared‑initial, single‑repair design made the preregistered detectable effect unattainable. We explain how these execution facts deterministically produce the null confirmatory outcome, document where the unique repair invocation appears in the archived provider trace, and provide artifact‑grounded design recommendations to enable future confirmatory detection of repair efficacy.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to assist or automate network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. While LLMs often produce plausible configuration fragments, prior work documents syntax, ordering, and semantic errors that threaten operational correctness and motivate guarded architectures combining generation with deterministic verification and targeted repair. However, the community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that pair explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration for confirmatory comparisons. To address this gap we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 to produce (1) a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) a snapshot deterministic validator implementing explicit intent constraint semantics, and (3) a preregistered paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass generator using a shared‑initial‑candidate design. The primary confirmatory question was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does a GVR pipeline materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Surveys and reviews report rapid growth in LLM applications for NetOps and highlight recurring challenges—hallucination, prompt injection, and the need for deterministic verification—that limit operational adoption [https://openalex.org/W4406137434; https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical studies show LLMs can draft device configurations but frequently commit syntax or semantic errors; several prototype systems combine generation with verification and iterative correction and report improved final correctness in focused settings (e.g., Mondal et al.; Jiang et al.) [https://openalex.org/W4388629193; https://openalex.org/W4388644518]. Security and adversarial analyses document prompt‑injection and jailbreak risks, reinforcing the need for guarded toolchains and rigorous validators [https://openalex.org/W4405181600; https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Despite these advances, existing evaluations are often dataset‑specific, involve human adjudication, or lack sealed, machine‑checkable confirmatory runs that bind a deterministic validator to an automated repair trigger under a fixed sampling plan. Our work contributes a sealed, archived, artifact‑complete proof‑of‑concept benchmark and a preregistered paired run that ties a snapshot deterministic validator to an automated repair trigger under a tightly specified repair budget and shared‑initial sampling policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary hypothesis. The preregistration fixed the paired, shared‑initial design, task generator, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness treatment, analysis executor, and a conservative repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Primary confirmatory hypothesis (H1): the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than the frozen single‑pass generator on N = 300 paired tasks (two‑sided α = 0.05). The estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference (guarded − baseline) and the preselected inferential test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval was pre‑registered (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729).

Task bank and validator semantics. A deterministic generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks per cluster). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, a difficulty label, and a required_sequence of atomic changes that must appear in any valid candidate. Device counts in the task bank range from 3–50 (manifested in representative task entries) and payloads use abstracted multi‑vendor device models. The snapshot deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implements the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation: it canonicalizes commands, enforces required_sequence and workflow policies (ordering, group and mutual‑exclusion constraints), applies allowed_fields and state‑preservation rules, computes the implied final_state, and returns a binary pass/fail plus diagnostic violation codes and a structured validator trace (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after diagnostics, repair_applied). These per‑task traces are recorded in the archived execution bundle and were used as the authoritative binary outcome for confirmatory analysis.

Paired, shared‑initial design and repair budget. To isolate repair value we used a shared initial generation per task: a single candidate was generated and supplied both as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline's initial candidate. The guarded condition validated that candidate and, only on validator failure, could invoke at most one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The orchestration intentionally prevented the guarded condition from sampling an independent alternative initial candidate; thus any guarded improvement could arise only from an invoked repair. This design reduces generator variance across conditions but constrains the maximal observable paired gain to the number of failed shared initial generations that the repair stage actually converts.

Model configuration, execution, and analysis plan. The declared model used in the run was gpt‑5‑mini executed via the hosted adapter with max_output_tokens = 2000, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, reasoning_effort = "minimal", provider = "openai_responses", store = false, and temperature = null. The planned episode count was 600 (two conditions × 300 tasks) with a preregistered completion threshold ≥90% (≥270 pairs) for confirmatory inference. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the estimand, performed the exact McNemar two‑sided test, and produced the paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). All execution and analysis steps were run under the sealed preregistration and the execution manifests, per‑task validator traces, provider call traces, and analysis artifacts are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The confirmatory run executed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, and model_calls_used = 301 (one shared initial generation per task: 300 calls; one repair call total). Provider call auditing reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 301 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}; all deterministic consistency checks passed in the reconciliation artifacts. The single repair‑stage hosted model call is the sole repair record and deterministically carries the discordant pair identifier (the unique n10 episode).

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated condition counts were baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966667) and guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299 (both passed), n10 = 1 (guarded pass, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline pass), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Per the preregistered analysis executor the exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and the paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01]. These numeric artifacts (condition_summary.csv and paired_contingency_table.csv) are archived and authoritative.

Representative diagnostics and locus of repair. Per‑task validator traces record validation_before/after diagnostics and repair_applied flags. Representative examples in the archived manifest show that many tasks labeled medium/hard (examples: shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) were satisfied by the shared initial generator under the fixed seeds and declared model release. The unique repair invocation appears as the only provider call with stage == "repair" in the provider trace; that record deterministically identifies the discordant episode for downstream qualitative inspection of repair input, repair prompt, and repair output.
sections.discussion:
Why the preregistered target effect was unattainable. The preregistered power calculation targeted detecting an absolute paired increase of 0.10 at N = 300. In paired binary designs only discordant pairs (n10 and n01) determine power and significance. Observed discordance (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) is insufficient to reject the null (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). More fundamentally, the realized marginal counts and the shared‑initial, single‑repair design arithmetically constrain the maximum achievable paired gain to the count of failed shared initial generations that the repair can convert. With baseline correctness at 299/300 and only one repair invocation executed, the largest possible paired difference is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333—exactly the observed estimate—so the predeclared target effect of 0.10 was unreachable given these execution facts.

Design and practical lessons for confirmatory trials. This execution demonstrates a deterministic interaction between generator quality, sampling design, and repair budget that must be addressed in confirmatory plans. When baseline correctness under deterministic single‑sample conditions is near ceiling, (A) a shared‑initial paired comparison with a strict single‑repair budget rarely yields sufficient discordance for statistical detection of practical repair benefits; (B) increasing detectable repair value requires (i) increasing initial failure prevalence (via harder tasks or adversarial seeds), (ii) permitting iterative repairs (maximum_repair_calls_per_task > 1), or (iii) allowing multiple independent initial generations per condition to evaluate selection/reranking rather than localized repair. Power calculations should be conditioned on plausible baseline marginals and on the operational repair policy; preregistered calculations that assume higher baseline failure rates risk being invalidated by realized marginals.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations. The archived artifacts support concrete, traceable design changes: (1) raise task difficulty or inject adversarial seeds so repair can run more often; (2) relax the per‑task repair budget to allow iterative repair chains; (3) permit multiple independent initial generations per task to evaluate selection/reranking efficacy; (4) adopt stateful/emulation validators that model ordered side effects and temporal constraints (beyond snapshot semantics) to expose additional failure modes; (5) include explicit adversarial test cases targeting prompt injection and hallucination. Each recommendation maps directly to recorded execution facts (high initial success rate, single repair invocation) and to per‑task diagnostics in the archive.

Threats to validity and operational implications. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but prevents the guarded condition from leveraging alternative initial samples; the single repair invocation materially limits contrasts for repair efficacy. Construct validity: the snapshot deterministic validator enforces specified intent constraints but omits vendor‑specific CLI idiosyncrasies and in‑flight temporal dynamics; stateful execution failure modes may be missed. External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and only one declared model release was evaluated; results do not generalize to production networks or other models without further experiments. Conclusion validity: the extremely small discordant count (n10 = 1) leaves subgroup and failure‑mode inference underpowered. Operational implication: when generator quality is near ceiling under deterministic single‑sample conditions and repair budgets are tightly constrained, localized repair yields negligible marginal gains; in lower‑reliability environments, adversarial inputs, iterative repair policies, or multi‑sample selection, GVR architectures are more likely to yield measurable benefits.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator, and performed a preregistered paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline against a frozen single‑pass gpt‑5‑mini generator on N = 300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported. This null confirmatory outcome is directly explained by an arithmetic ceiling produced by a near‑perfect baseline together with minimal repair engagement (the guarded repair stage executed only once). We release the archived preregistration, execution manifest, provider call traces, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the community can instantiate harder settings—higher difficulty, iterative repair, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons—that will reveal when generate–validate–repair pipelines yield measurable operational value.

disclosure_statement: This study followed the sealed preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 and used an archived initial master prompt. The initial master prompt is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt (immutable SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Declared model and generation settings used in the execution were: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. Orchestration implemented the shared initial generation (one shared call per task) and the guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline with maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implementing scoring rule "full_intent_constraint_validation"; per‑task scorer outputs and validator traces are archived in the execution bundle. Preregistered analysis executor performed exact McNemar testing and a paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Execution accounting (authoritative) recorded planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, and model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call). Provider call auditing records stage counts of 300 shared_initial_generation calls and exactly 1 repair call; the single repair is the sole repair‑stage hosted model call in the archived provider trace and carries the discordant episode identifier. Human role and autonomy: a human Research Director selected the topic family and provided pre‑lock constraints and the initial master prompt; after the autonomy lock the autonomous pipeline performed literature synthesis, study selection, sealed preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Construct validity: the deterministic validator enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt‑5‑mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N = 300 tasks, so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10 = 1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archived model configuration and per‑call provider traces.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle and are authoritative for auditors.
